narrative.text: The cover page of the July 2018 WHO technical report on HIV diagnosis and ARV use in HIV-exposed infants, a programmatic update.
The copyright and cataloguing page, with the document number, Creative Commons licence terms, suggested citation and standard WHO disclaimers.

Gives the executive summary, explaining that few countries have adopted the 2016 WHO innovations of birth testing, point-of-care NAT and enhanced postnatal prophylaxis, and that this update draws on 2017 and 2018 expert meetings to describe changing strategies for infant HIV. It is followed by a list of abbreviations.

Describes the status of paediatric HIV, noting the drop in new child infections under the Global Plan but 180 000 new infections in 2017, and the shift of mother-to-child transmission towards the postnatal period. A figure shows early and later transmission rates in the priority countries of the Start Free, Stay Free, AIDS Free framework.

Notes that only about half of children living with HIV were on treatment in 2017 and that untreated infants face very high mortality, then sets out the reasons for this technical update. It explains that falling transmission rates and low viremia have reduced the predictive value of nucleic acid tests, so false-positive infant diagnoses are increasingly reported. The page raises the question of introducing an indeterminate result range for early infant diagnosis.

Reports a systematic review indicating that a sizeable share of non-negative infant test results are indeterminate, most of which prove negative on retesting, and explains the use of PCR cycle thresholds to define an indeterminate range. It closes with definitions of terms such as indeterminate, non-negative and discordant results.

Discusses confirmatory testing, noting that prequalified point-of-care infant diagnosis devices perform comparably to laboratory tests and can be used to confirm positive results, and covers management of discordant results and treatment interruption. A summary box stresses immediate retesting of indeterminate results, team support for repeated cases and confirmatory testing of all positives.

Covers the rollout of point-of-care early infant diagnosis, citing studies in Malawi and Mozambique showing faster results and earlier treatment, and lists lessons on device placement and site selection. It also addresses birth testing, and a box urges national regulators to approve the two prequalified technologies quickly.

Summarizes challenges of HIV testing at birth, such as staffing, sampling newborns and linkage to treatment, and describes country experiences in South Africa and Kenya. It stresses linking infected newborns to treatment with suitable formulations and the need for good leadership and coordination.
A blank page with no extractable text.

Addresses interpretation of the 9-month infant test and simplification of the testing algorithm, explaining how maternal treatment, infant prophylaxis and late maternal infection can make rapid antibody tests unreliable for exposure or infection status. It sets out key points: testing mothers to establish exposure, not treating a negative infant result after 4 months as definitive, and confirming positive results with NAT.

Explains the WHO recommendation of dual AZT and nevirapine prophylaxis for high-risk infants, extended to 12 weeks in breastfeeding infants, and defines which infants are high risk. It discusses the rationale based on mothers reaching viral suppression and gives guidance on whether to continue infant prophylaxis when maternal adherence is poor. It advises that prophylaxis, once stopped, should not be restarted and that attention should go to the causes of poor maternal adherence.

Considers giving high-risk infants presumptive triple-drug treatment as enhanced prophylaxis, paired with testing before it starts, and describes the limited and complex options for early infant treatment. It weighs the use of fixed-dose combination tablets, noting issues such as unwanted lamivudine exposure and the need to split tablets into quarters.

Discusses integrating care for HIV-exposed infants into maternal and child health services and linked information systems, while noting pressure on staff. It also describes the role of community services and networks of women living with HIV, and lists patient-level and health system interventions to keep infants in the testing cascade.

Lists key research questions on infant diagnosis, prophylaxis and treatment, such as the value of birth testing and an indeterminate range and the dosing of new ARVs for newborns. A closing section calls for strengthening existing systems, tailoring strategies to context and gathering more programme evidence.
An acknowledgements page listing the meeting participants and their institutions and the WHO staff involved.
Part of the reference list, citing studies on indeterminate PCR results, confirmatory and point-of-care infant testing in southern Africa, and related WHO documents.
Annex 1, a standard operating procedure flowchart for managing indeterminate early infant diagnosis results, including retesting within 4 weeks and team review of repeated indeterminate results.

Annex 2, a diagram for managing discordant results and treatment interruption, with infant NAT and viral load testing at 4 weeks, 4 months and 8 months after stopping ART and different scenarios depending on when breastfeeding ends.

Annex 3, a simplified algorithm for early infant HIV diagnosis from birth to 18 months, showing when to do NAT and antibody tests and when to start ART. It lists key principles such as testing the mother to assess exposure and doing NAT at 9 months, with notes on final diagnosis after breastfeeding ends.
Annex 4, an algorithm for classifying infants as high or low risk at delivery based on the mother's HIV status, time on ART and viral load, to decide between standard and enhanced prophylaxis.

Annex 5, a table comparing syrup, tablet and fixed-dose combination options for AZT and nevirapine infant prophylaxis over 0–12 weeks, with doses and pros and cons of each. It notes that AZT has no separate prophylactic dose and that presumptive treatment should follow age-appropriate WHO dosing.
A blank page with no extractable text.
The back cover, giving contact details for the WHO Department of HIV/AIDS in Geneva and the document number.
